cards.text: Job has just poured his heart out, asking God why He considers him His enemy (Job 13:24). Now Eliphaz the Temanite, one of the three friends who came to comfort Job (Job 2:11), replies. Friend, I can already tell this is NOT a cookie-basket kind of visit.

cards.question: Eliphaz opens by asking if a wise man would answer with empty counsel or fill his belly with the hot east wind. What is he saying about Job's speeches?

cards.text: Eliphaz isn't done. He tells Job he even undermines the fear of God, and that his iniquity is what instructs his mouth. Whew. Two verses in, friend, and I'm sweating for Job.

cards.question: Eliphaz says he doesn't need to accuse Job, because Job's own ___ condemns him.

cards.text: Then Eliphaz asks Job if he was the first man ever born, brought forth before the hills. I've been called worn out before, friend, but NOBODY ever asked me if I was older than a HILL.

cards.question: Eliphaz asks Job if he listens in on the council of God, or keeps wisdom to himself. What is Eliphaz's point?

answers.text: Job is older than all of them

cards.text: Eliphaz has backup, and he wants Job to know it: the gray-haired and the aged are on his side. That's walking into an argument and holding up your whole group chat as witnesses.

cards.question: Eliphaz says the gray-haired men on his side are much older than Job's father.

cards.text: Eliphaz asks, “Are the consolations of God not enough for you, even words spoken gently to you?” I'll be honest, friend. If somebody opened with hot east wind at me, I'd still be waiting on the gentle part.

cards.question: Eliphaz asks Job why his heart has carried him away and why his eyes flash. What does Eliphaz say Job is doing?

cards.text: Then Eliphaz zooms out to everybody: “What is man, that he should be pure, or one born of woman, that he should be righteous?” And “born of woman” is a phrase Job just used himself (Job 14:1).

cards.question: Eliphaz says God puts complete trust in His holy ones.
Eliphaz says if even the heavens aren't pure in God's eyes, how much less man, who is vile and corrupt and drinks ___ like water.

cards.text: Eliphaz says, “Listen to me and I will inform you.” When somebody opens like that, friend, pull up a chair, because he's about to pass down what wise men declared from their fathers.

cards.question: Eliphaz is ready to share what the wise men passed down. Who is this teaching all about?

cards.text: Eliphaz says the wicked man writhes in pain all his days. Sounds of terror fill his ears.

cards.question: Eliphaz says the destroyer waits until the wicked man is poor to attack him.

cards.text: He despairs of his return from darkness, and he wanders about as food for vultures. Friend, I spent years in the dark at the back of a junk drawer, and I'll say this: at least we didn't have VULTURES.
Eliphaz goes on: “Distress and anguish terrify him, overwhelming him like a king poised to attack.”

cards.question: Eliphaz gives the reason behind all this trouble. What does he say the wicked man has done?

answers.text: Stretched out his hand against God

cards.question: Eliphaz pictures the wicked man rushing headlong at God with a thick, studded shield.

cards.text: Charging at the Almighty with a shield. That's squaring up to a hurricane with an umbrella, friend. Then Eliphaz says the wicked man looks well fed, but hold on.

cards.question: Eliphaz says the wicked man will dwell in ___ cities, in abandoned houses destined to become rubble.
Eliphaz says the wicked man's wealth will endure and spread across the land.

cards.text: He won't escape from the darkness. Eliphaz says the flame will wither his shoots, and “the breath of God’s mouth will carry him away.”

cards.question: Eliphaz warns the wicked man not to deceive himself by trusting in emptiness. Why not?

answers.text: God will fill it for him

cards.text: It'll all be “paid in full before his time.” Then Eliphaz paints a picture: “He will be like a vine stripped of its unripe grapes, like an olive tree that sheds its blossoms.”

cards.question: Eliphaz pictures a vine losing its unripe grapes and an olive tree shedding its blossoms. What is he saying about the wicked man?

cards.text: Eliphaz says the company of the godless will be barren, and fire will consume the tents of bribery.

cards.question: Eliphaz says the godless conceive ___ and give birth to ___.

cards.text: Their womb is pregnant with deceit, Eliphaz says, and that's the end of his speech. Grab a cookie and stretch, friend, because this conversation is far from over.

findings.problem: Stop 2, card 14 quotes "paid in full before his time.", which isn't the exact BSB wording.

rule.text: Quotes: Quotation marks around Bible words mean the exact BSB wording, punctuation included.

findings.problem: The question says Job 'keeps wisdom to himself.' Job 15:8 says 'limit wisdom to yourself,' which means claiming wisdom belongs only to you. 'Keeps wisdom to himself' means not sharing it, which is a different meaning from what the text says.

rule.text: Retelling: Papa Dorin can retell in his own words and fill in what the text clearly implies. Scene-setting details are fine. He never says anything the text shows is wrong.

findings.problem: The card cites Job 15:17-19 but tells nothing from verse 19 (the land given to them alone, with no foreigner among them). The citation is wider than what the card uses.

rule.text: Every story card cites the verses it tells, from the first verse it uses to the last, no wider and no narrower.

findings.problem: The card opens with 'Charging at the Almighty with a shield,' which is Job 15:26, but it cites only Job 15:27. The citation is narrower than what the card uses.

rule.text: Every story card cites the verses it tells, from the first verse it uses to the last, no wider and no narrower.

findings.problem: The question says 'Eliphaz warns the wicked man.' Job 15:31 is in the third person ('Let him not deceive himself'), spoken to Job about the wicked man, not addressed to him. The card names who is being spoken to when the text doesn't.

rule.text: Leave open what the text leaves open: who is being spoken to, why, or how two things connect.

findings.problem: The two-blank question 'conceive ___ and give birth to ___' has 'trouble' and 'evil' as the right words. They fit either blank equally well. Putting them in the right order means guessing the exact wording of the line, not reasoning out its meaning, and a baker could argue that the swapped order is right.

rule.text: The rule against guessing the next words of a line (see below) applies to every passage, and to fill in the blank too. The blank tests meaning the baker can reason out, not wording they haven't seen.

findings.problem: Several story cards in stop 2 (cards 3, 6, 12 and 16) are bare paraphrase or bare quotation with no trace of Papa Dorin's voice. Card 6 is only a quote. Together they make the second half read like a plain recitation.

rule.text: Short, but not stripped down. A story card still has enough of Papa Dorin's voice and enough context that the moment makes sense.
